Home Coffee Roasting Basics

Roasting is the key step that turns green beans into coffee. Green beans are grassy and pale; only after heating do they develop the aroma and color we know. This article covers the basics of home roasting so first-timers know what to watch for.

Equipment you need

The simplest way to roast at home is with a frying pan or a hand-held mesh roaster; a small roasting machine is the next step up. You also need a timer, a thermometer, and a sieve or electric fan for cooling. Roasting produces a lot of smoke and chaff, so do it somewhere well ventilated.

Roasting stages

When heated, green beans first go through a drying phase, turning from green to yellow and smelling like bread. Next comes the Maillard phase, where the color gradually turns brown. At higher temperature the beans make the first crack, at which point they are already a drinkable light roast. Further heating leads to the second crack, where oil starts to appear on the surface: a dark roast.

Storing roasted beans

Freshly roasted beans keep releasing carbon dioxide, so let them rest one to three days before brewing for a more stable flavor. Store them in bags with a one-way valve in a cool, dry place; avoid the fridge, because the temperature change when taking them out makes the beans absorb moisture.
